title: What is observable
objective: Choose the observations of a command, aborts included, define observational equivalence, and state the preservation theorem in CompCert's template, then produce a pair of runs that a weak observer equates and a client tells apart.

blocks.md: A compiler's theorem says the compiled program behaves like the source. "Behaves" does all the work: it names what a client may see, and anything it leaves out can change without breaking the theorem. This lesson picks that list for the compiler you are building, and shows what a weak list lets through.

choice.prompt: A compiler turns a failed funds check into "change nothing, report success". Your theorem compares final balances only. Does it catch the bug?

options.why: The balances end equal either way. Only the outcome differs.
A source that aborts leaves the balances as they were, and so does the compiled program that does nothing.
Neither run writes anything.

choice.prompt: Which is part of CompCert's observable behavior?

options.why: The manual excludes it by name, together with memory consumption.
The manual excludes it by name, together with execution time.

options.text: The trace of input and output, and how the program ends
options.why: Termination, divergence or going wrong, plus the trace of input and output (Leroy 2009, section 2.1).
It is an artifact, not a behavior.

blocks.md:
A client of your system sends a command and sees an outcome: the command committed, or it aborted with an error code. An observation is a function of the starting store and that outcome. Two runs are observationally equivalent when no observation tells them apart. The weaker the observation, the more programs count as equal, and the easier the theorem is to prove.

Take the compiler of SP-9.3. It turns the funds check into conditional writes, `writeIf`, that match nothing when funds are short, so a transfer that should abort commits and changes nothing. Run it on a store with balance 0 and a transfer of 1, under two observers: balances only, and the outcome, which is the committed balances or the error code.

blocks.direction: Each observer is applied to the source's run and to the compiled run. The pair view lists what each observer sees in both, and marks the observers that tell them apart.

code.text:
source    transfer 1 a1 a2
store     (a1, a2) = (0, 0)

compiled by SP-9.3's scheme (the positivity check is unchanged and left out):
  ldi      r0 1
  read     r1 a1
  sub      r2 r1 r0
  writeIf  r1 r0 a1 r2     # debit only when the balance covers the amount
  read     r3 a2
  add      r3 r3 r0
  writeIf  r1 r0 a2 r3     # credit only when the same condition holds

observers  balances only | outcome

call.prompt: Which observers tell these two runs apart?

options.why: One run aborts and the other commits.
Both runs leave the balances unchanged.
It sees an abort in one run and a commit in the other.
The balances-only observer equates the two runs.

blocks.after: The balances are equal, so the balances-only observer equates the runs, and the outcome observer does not {{run:RUN-lean-abort-blind}}. This is S6's unchecked rowcount one level up: an observer that cannot see aborts lets a proof pass over that bug.

choice.prompt: An observer merges error codes: an abort reports only "failed". A compiler reports `insufficient` for a non-positive amount, where the source says `nonPositive`. Which command and store give runs that the observer equates and a client tells apart?

options.why: Both runs commit with (5, 5). Nothing differs, so no client tells them apart.
The source aborts with `nonPositive` and the compiled program with `insufficient`. Merged codes equate the runs, and a client that reads the code does not.
Both abort with `insufficient`, so the runs agree on the code too.
Merging codes hides exactly this kind of difference.

blocks.md:
CompCert states what it proves in one sentence: if the compiler produces the code, then the observable behavior of that code improves on one of the allowed observable behaviors of the source (manual, section 1.2). In Coq it is one line, `transf_c_program p = OK tp -> backward_simulation (Csem.semantics p) (Asm.semantics tp)` (`driver/Compiler.v`, read 2026-10-23). "Improves on" matters when the source can go wrong, because undefined behavior lets the compiler pick any behavior. Your fragment has none, since errors are outcomes, so "improves on" becomes equality. The theorem for your fragment:

```lean
theorem preservation (c : Cmd) (p : List Instr) :
    compile c = some p →
    ∀ (s : Store) (regs : Regs), obs s (runT p regs s) = obs s (runS c s)
```

The premise `compile c = some p` says the compiler produced `p`. A compiler that never produces anything never meets it.

blocks.direction: Replay shows: `Preserves`, the compiler that returns `none` for every command, and its proof. Look at what the proof never touches.

code.text:
def Preserves {Cmd Prog Obs : Type} (compile : Cmd → Option Prog)
    (obsS : Cmd → Obs) (obsT : Prog → Obs) : Prop :=
  ∀ c p, compile c = some p → obsT p = obsS c

-- a "compiler" that refuses every command
def refuse {Cmd Prog : Type} : Cmd → Option Prog := fun _ => none

theorem refuse_preserves {Cmd Prog Obs : Type} (obsS : Cmd → Obs) (obsT : Prog → Obs) :
    Preserves (refuse : Cmd → Option Prog) obsS obsT := by
  unfold Preserves
  intro c p h
  simp [refuse] at h

call.prompt: A "compiler" returns `none` for every command. Does it satisfy the theorem?

options.why: The premise `compile c = some p` never holds, so the implication holds for every command.
A false premise makes an implication true.

options.text: Only if every source command aborts.
options.why: No compiled program exists to run, so nothing is compared.

blocks.after: The proof is one line, and it never mentions an observation {{run:RUN-lean-preservation-frag}}. The template needs a companion: the compiler accepts every command of the fragment. That companion is `compile_complete`, which you prove in LAB-9.10, and it is the lesson on vacuous premises from S1 again.

options.text: Whenever the source commits, the compiled program commits with the same balances.
options.why: Equal observations include the outcome and every balance, once `obs` sees aborts, error codes and balances.

options.text: The compiler accepts every command of the fragment.
options.why: That is `compile_complete`, a separate theorem.

options.text: The compiled program takes as many steps as the source.
options.why: Steps lie outside the observation.
They abort exactly when the source does, with the same error.

blocks.md: Preservation says nothing about what the observation leaves out. CompCert's list is explicit: execution time and memory consumption are excluded. Yours is the same kind of list. The steps the compiled program takes, the registers it uses and the stores it passes through all lie outside the outcome observation. That is a design choice, and it is also a place for a later problem to hide.

blocks.direction: The pair view runs the source and both compiled programs from the store above, and shows each observer's view of all three.

code.text:
source      transfer 5 a1 a2
store       (a1, a2) = (10, 0)

compiled A  the reference compiler's output
compiled B  the same output with one redundant `read` before its first write

observers   outcome | steps

call.prompt: Preservation holds under the outcome observation. Which of these can still differ between the source run and a compiled run?

options.why: They are inside the observation.
It is inside the observation.
Aborts are observed, so this cannot differ.
Steps, registers and intermediate stores lie outside the observation, as CompCert's time and memory do.

blocks.after: Both compiled programs commit with the same balances, and one takes more steps {{run:RUN-tv-reference}}. What an observation leaves out comes back in S9.L9.

choice.prompt: Compiled B is the reference output plus one redundant `read` before its first write. Which command and store give runs that are equal under the outcome observation and different in steps?

options.why: Both commit with (5, 5), and B runs one more instruction.
Both abort with `insufficient` at the guard, before the redundant `read`, so the step counts match.

options.text: A store where B ends with different balances from the source
options.why: The extra `read` changes no write, so no such store exists.
Preservation makes the outcomes equal and says nothing about steps.

choice.prompt: An observer maps every abort to the balances the run started with. A compiler turns a failed funds check into "change nothing, report success". Which command and store give runs that the observer equates and a client tells apart?

options.why: Both runs commit with (5, 5), so there is nothing to tell apart.
The source aborts, and the observer reports the starting balances. The compiled program commits with the same balances. A client sees an error in one run and success in the other.
A self-transfer nets to zero in both runs, and both commit.
The observer still sees the balances, but not the abort that separates these runs.

choice.prompt: Which statement about `preservation` and `compile_complete` is true?

options.text: Without `compile_complete`, `preservation` still holds for a compiler that refuses every command.
options.why: The premise never holds, so the implication holds vacuously.

options.text: `preservation` implies that the compiler accepts every command.
options.why: It says nothing about commands the compiler refuses.
Aborts are observed, so it covers them too.

options.text: `preservation` forbids the compiled program from using extra registers.
options.why: Registers lie outside the observation.

blocks.title: Production twin
blocks.md: CompCert's `transf_c_program_correct` and manual section 1.2, pinned in {{run:RUN-twin-pins}}. What does `= OK tp` exclude? Which simulation direction does the theorem state? Which phases does the manual call unverified?

blocks.title: Build this
blocks.md: In LAB-9.4 you write `obs` and the matching relation R in your own statement module. The check holds them to a floor: aborts, error codes and every balance must be observable, and R must imply equal observations. The next lesson draws the diagram that R belongs to.
